analysis.one_liner: Eliminates interest on federal student loans and caps new rates at 4%.
analysis.headline: The bill to wipe out interest on federal student loans was referred to the Senate education committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal student loans so that no interest accrues: starting July 1, 2024, existing federal Direct Loans would automatically be modified to 0% interest, and older federal loans still held by banks (FFEL and Perkins loans) would be refinanced into no-interest federal loans with no origination fees. New loans would carry a low, income-based rate between 0% and 4%. All loan repayments would flow into a new Education Affordability Trust Fund invested in bonds, whose profits would pay the loan program's administrative costs, with any extra going to supplemental Pell Grants.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of current federal student loan borrowers would stop accruing interest on their debt, meaning every payment they make goes to principal instead of partially to interest charges. Borrowers with older bank-held federal loans would be refinanced into the same no-interest terms without paying an origination fee, and their prior payments would still count toward income-driven forgiveness. Future students would borrow at 0-4% depending on family income relative to their local median income, and could borrow more per year; Pell Grant recipients could eventually receive supplemental grants if the trust fund earns more than it needs.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Education Department to automatically modify every eligible federal Direct Loan so that no interest accrues beginning July 1, 2024, unless a borrower opts out.

Refinances eligible non-Direct federal loans — such as bank-held FFEL and Perkins loans — into no-interest federal Direct Consolidation Loans with no origination fees, and preserves the borrower's prior payment history toward income-driven repayment forgiveness.

Replaces the current rate-setting formula for new loans with a tiered rate from 0% to 4%, based on the borrower's income relative to the local area median income, so lower- and middle-income borrowers pay 0%.

Raises annual and aggregate federal borrowing limits and indexes them to inflation, and directs all loan repayments into a new Education Affordability Trust Fund whose investment profits would cover the program's administrative costs, with excess used for supplemental Pell Grants and grants to colleges that keep tuition growth under 3%.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government — and ultimately taxpayers — would forgo the interest income it currently collects on its roughly $1.6 trillion student loan portfolio, which today counts as federal revenue. The bill's trust fund is designed to cover only administrative costs from bond-investment profits, and its transfer formula drops to 10% or even 0% of profits in lean years, so it would not come close to replacing the lost interest stream. Critics would also warn that colleges capture some of the benefit: cheaper and larger federal loans can enable institutions to keep raising tuition.

drawbacks.text: Forgone interest is a real federal cost: interest payments on federal loans currently flow back to the Treasury and reduce the deficit, and the bill's trust fund would transfer only a share of its bond profits (anywhere from 100% down to 0% depending on profit tiers), nowhere near replacing the lost interest revenue.

The bill raises annual and aggregate loan limits while making borrowing nearly free, which could enable colleges to keep raising tuition — the long-standing concern that easier federal credit is captured by institutions — though the supplemental grant program does condition eligibility on keeping tuition growth under 3%.

In dollar terms, borrowers with the largest balances — often graduate borrowers and higher-income professionals — would save the most, though the income-tiered 0-4% rates for new loans and the area-median-income thresholds temper that somewhat.

The trust fund is an untested structure: a six-member board would invest repayments in municipal, Treasury, agency, international, and corporate bonds, and if profits fall below $300 million per period nothing is transferred to the loan program at all, adding market risk to a core federal program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of households carrying federal student debt, ending interest is a substantial, concrete benefit — every payment reduces principal, and debts stop growing for people who cannot pay. The cost is genuine: the federal government would give up a large interest revenue stream with no replacement funding, and easier credit could feed tuition inflation at the margin. The trust-fund design is creative but adds investment risk and complexity to what is now a straightforward government program. It was a serious, detailed proposal whose fiscal price and design questions were never weighed on the record because it never received a single hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Peter Welch introduced the Student Loan Interest Elimination Act on July 27, 2023, with one Democratic cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee — and that was the last action ever taken on it.
The bill received no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, at which point the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: the federal Treasury continues collecting interest on federal student loans, and borrowers keep paying it. Student loan servicers and the existing loan system keep their current roles.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Treasury and the existing loan system

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote after it was referred, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's two sponsors were both Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but because it never reached a committee vote or the floor, the partisan split was never actually tested.

industries.note: The bill keeps the federal loan program running and services it through the Education Department, with servicers' administrative costs paid out of trust fund profits rather than eliminated. Their role in the system is locked in even as borrower interest charges end.

industries.industry: Banks and finance companies holding older FFEL student loans
industries.note: The bill would pay off their remaining loans in full — principal, accrued interest, and late charges — giving them immediate cash but ending their future interest income stream. Borrowers traded a private-held federal loan for a cheaper federal one.

Near-free federal credit and higher loan limits make it easier for students to pay rising tuition, but the bill's supplemental Pell and student-success grants are limited to institutions that keep tuition growth at or under 3% per year, a direct brake on price increases.
